ce:caption.ce:simple-para: Timeline of key discoveries and pathways in ferroptosis regulation. Early studies on oxytosis (1989) highlighted a vulnerability related to GSH/ ROS, foreshadowing the concept of ferroptosis. In 2003, erastin-induced cell death was reported to be iron-dependent, leading to the formal definition of ferroptosis in 2012. Subsequent research identified system Xc⁻ inhibition and GPX4 inactivation (2014) as critical drivers of lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis. The role of ACSL4-mediated polyunsaturated fatty acid–phospholipid (PUFA–PL) synthesis (2016) emerged as a pivotal susceptibility pathway. More recent studies have uncovered GPX4-independent lipid antioxidant mechanisms, including the FSP1–coenzyme Q10 (FSP1–CoQ10) axis (2019), the GCH1–BH4 pathway (2020), and DHODH-mediated mitochondrial CoQ10 recycling (2021). Notably, vitamin K was identified as a potent ferroptosis inhibitor (2022). Collectively, these discoveries have significantly advanced our understanding of lipid-based cell death and its regulation.

Integrated antioxidant defense systems against ferroptosis: GPX4-dependent and GPX4-independent mechanisms. (A) The canonical cystine/glutamate antiporter System Xc⁻ and GPX4-centered antioxidant axis suppress ferroptosis by eliminating lipid hydroperoxides. System Xc⁻, composed of SLC7A11 and SLC3A2, imports extracellular cystine (CyS₂) in exchange for intracellular glutamate (Glu). Cystine is reduced to cysteine (CyS), a precursor for GSH biosynthesis catalyzed by glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCL) and glutathione synthetase (GSS). GPX4 utilizes GSH to convert phospholipid hydroperoxides (PUFAs-OOH) into nontoxic lipid alcohols (PUFAs-OH) through a catalytic redox cycle involving selenocysteine (Sec), thereby preventing membrane damage. Inhibitors such as Erastin and RSL3 induce ferroptosis by disrupting SLC7A11 or inactivating GPX4, respectively. (B) Three GPX4-independent radical-trapping antioxidant systems counteract ferroptosis by scavenging lipid peroxyl radicals. FSP1, localized to the plasma membrane, reduces CoQ10 to ubiquinol (CoQ10H₂) using NAD(P)H, which neutralizes lipid radicals. In mitochondria, DHODH catalyzes the reduction of CoQ10 to CoQ10H₂ to suppress lipid peroxidation. Additionally, the GCH1–BH4 pathway protects cells by producing BH4, a lipophilic antioxidant that inhibits ferroptosis and facilitates phospholipid remodeling. Together, these systems operate independently of GPX4 and GSH metabolism to maintain redox homeostasis.

Complementary cellular defense mechanisms against ferroptosis: lipid remodeling, membrane repair, and iron regulation. (A) Monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) resist peroxidation due to the lack of bis-allylic sites. SCD1 converts saturated fatty acids into MUFAs, which are activated by acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 3 (ACSL3) and incorporated into phospholipids by MBOAT1/2. This lipid remodeling displaces polyunsaturated fatty acid-phospholipids (PUFA-PLs), reducing peroxidation and conferring GPX4-independent ferroptosis resistance. (B) The endosomal sorting complex required for transport III (ESCRT-III) repairs peroxidized membranes. Lipid peroxidation-triggered calcium influx recruits CHMP5/6, which are components of ESCRT-III, to damaged sites, limiting ROS-induced rupture and ferroptosis. (C) Iron metabolism shapes ferroptosis sensitivity. Transferrin-bound ferric iron (Fe³⁺) is taken up via TFR1, reduced by STEAP3, and imported into the labile iron pool (LIP) through divalent metal transporter-1 (DMT1) and Zinc transporter zinc-and iron-related protein 8 (ZIP8/14). Iron is stored in ferritin (FTH1/FTL), exported via ferroportin, and regulated by IREB2. Heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1) releases free iron, promoting Fenton chemistry and lipid peroxidation.

NRF2-mediated transcriptional regulation of antioxidant and anti-ferroptotic pathways. Under basal conditions, NRF2 is targeted for degradation by three major E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes:(A) KEAP1-CUL3-RBX1, (B) SCF/β-TrCP, (C) Synoviolin/Hrd1, and (D) NRF2-mediated transcriptional activation of antiferroptotic programs. Upon escape from degradation (via A/B/C inhibition), stabilized NRF2 translocates to the nucleus, dimerizes with sMaf, and binds the Antioxidant Response Element (ARE). This drives expression of target genes across three functional categories: Glutathione synthesis, metabolism (e.g.,GCLC, GCLM, GSS, SLC7A11, GPX4, GSTs), Intermediate metabolism (e.g., G6PD, PPARG, AKR1C1, ALDH1A1) for NADPH regeneration and detoxification, Iron metabolism (e.g., FTH1, FTL, SLC40A1, HMOX1, FECH). Collectively, these pathways mitigate lipid peroxidation and suppress ferroptosis.

Metabolic and biochemical pathways influencing ferroptosis sensitivity: PUFA-PL synthesis, regulation of lipid peroxidation, and iron metabolism and toxicity. (A) Polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA)-phospholipids (PLs) serve as key substrates for ferroptosis. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) initiates PUFA synthesis, followed by activation by ACSL4 and incorporation into PLs by lysophosphatidylcholine acyltransferase 3 (LPCAT3). Peroxisomes support this process via plasmalogen biosynthesis. Phospholipase A2 group VI (iPLA2β) removes oxidized PUFA tails, while D-PUFAs inhibit peroxidation. (B) Regulation of Lipid Peroxidation: Lipid peroxidation, a hallmark of ferroptosis, is driven by lipoxygenases (ALOXs) and cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase (POR), producing phospholipid hydroperoxides (PL-PUFA-OOH). If not reduced by GPX4, these peroxides accumulate and disrupt membrane integrity. Iron-catalyzed Fenton reactions further amplify peroxidation. (C) Iron metabolism shapes ferroptosis sensitivity. TFR1 imports ferric iron (Fe³⁺), which is reduced by six-transmembrane epithelial antigen of prostate 3 (STEAP3) and stored in ferritin (FTL, FTH1). Ferritinophagy via nuclear receptor coactivator 4 (NCOA4) and mitochondrial transport by SLC25A37/28 modulate the labile iron pool (LIP). Excess Fe²⁺ is exported via SLC40A1.

Oncogenic and microenvironmental regulation of ferroptosis sensitivity: roles of tumor suppressors, hypoxia, and mesenchymal transition. (A) Tumor suppressors such as p53 and BAP1 enhance ferroptosis sensitivity through transcriptional repression of SLC7A11, limiting cystine uptake and GSH synthesis. p53 also induces p21 to maintain GSH and reduce lipid peroxidation, while mutant forms (e.g., P53-R270H) impair this regulation. (B) Hypoxia-induced stabilization of HIF1α and HIF2α promotes PUFA accumulation, phospholipid peroxidation (via ACSL4 and PTGS2), and represses antioxidant defense (e.g., GSH) partly through SLC7A11 downregulation and XBP1-mediated transcriptional programs. (C) Mesenchymal-like cancer cell states, including persister cells post therapy, exhibit ACSL4-driven lipid remodeling and increased PUFA content, leading to GPX4 dependency and ferroptosis vulnerability. This metabolic rewiring is partly driven by ZEB1 and may create a therapeutic opportunity.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Programmed cell death (PCD) is a fundamental biological process that plays a critical role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and modulating the effectiveness of cancer therapies. Among the various forms of PCD, ferroptosis has recently attracted considerable attention as a promising strategy to overcome therapeutic resistance, which often limits the success of conventional treatments such as chemotherapy. This review delves into the molecular mechanisms underlying the susceptibility of different cell types to ferroptosis, highlighting the pathways involved and the diverse cellular responses triggered by therapeutic interventions. We also explore various strategies to enhance ferroptosis sensitivity in cancer cells, including the manipulation of cell therapy, transcription factors, regulatory genes, ion homeostasis, organelle functions, and the extracellular environment. Additionally, we examine current and emerging therapeutic agents targeting ferroptosis, discussing their clinical potential and prospects for integration into cancer treatment regimens. By reviewing both the underlying mechanisms and therapeutic approaches related to ferroptosis, this article aims to provide valuable insights into how targeting this unique form of cell death may help address tumor resistance and improve patient outcomes.

ce:section.ce:para: The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) Biennial Report 2020–2021, published by the World Health Organization (WHO), highlights cancer as a pressing global health challenge, marked by persistently high incidence rates and an increasing prevalence worldwide. In China, cancer has become one of the most prevalent diseases, characterized by unique epidemiological features and distinct patient demographics [1]. As a heterogeneous disease driven by dysregulated cell death pathways, cancer imposes a substantial and growing burden on global health systems [2]. Understanding the mechanisms of tumorigenesis and advancing therapeutic strategies that target and induce tumor cell death remain an urgent priority. Researchers are exploring the genetic mutations that drive cancer progression, such as alterations in the TP53 gene, as well as the influence of the tumor microenvironment in promoting therapeutic resistance. Current therapeutic strategies are advancing by targeting key molecules involved in tumor growth and by developing approaches to overcome resistance, including the use of agents that induce programmed cell death (PCD) and combination therapies that simultaneously target both the tumor cells and their supportive microenvironment.

Over the past decade, the Nomenclature Committee on Cell Death (NCCD) has provided a standardized framework for defining and classifying cell death, integrating morphological, biochemical, and functional parameters, including intrinsic apoptosis, extrinsic apoptosis, ferroptosis, mitochondrial permeability transition (MPT)-driven necrosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, parthanatos, entotic cell death, NETotic cell death, lysosome-dependent cell death, autophagy-dependent cell death, immunogenic cell death, cellular senescence, and mitotic catastrophe. Historically viewed as a passive and inevitable consequence of cellular life, cell death is now understood to involve genetically regulated programs that selectively eliminate superfluous, damaged, or potentially dangerous cells. This paradigm shift, supported by extensive experimental evidence, has significantly deepened our understanding of the molecular underpinnings of cell death and its role in health and disease [3–7].

PCD is a genetically regulated process encompassing several well-characterized modalities, including apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, PANoptosis, and autophagy-dependent cell death. More recently, novel PCD mechanisms such as cuproptosis[8] and triaptosis [9] have been identified, expanding our understanding of cell death regulation. These PCD pathways play a crucial role in controlling tumorigenesis, tumor progression and tumor treatment. Increasing evidence indicates that resistance to PCD is a hallmark of cancer development, and a deeper understanding of these mechanisms is informing various targeted therapeutic strategies against tumors. Pharmacological targeting of specific PCD pathways using small-molecule compounds has emerged as a promising cancer approach, with significant advances achieved across multiple cancer types [10]. Different lethal pathways influence tumor behavior and therapeutic sensitivity. During the early stages of tumorigenesis, genetic or epigenetic alterations may confer therapeutic resistance to cancer cells by disrupting PCD signaling pathways, making evasion of cell death a defining feature of malignant tumors. Interestingly, therapeutic modulation of one or more PCD pathways, either independently or synergistically, holds promise for overcoming resistance and restoring therapeutic sensitivity [11].

Ferroptosis is a recently characterized form of PCD marked by iron accumulation and lipid peroxidation. Growing evidence implicates ferroptosis in the pathogenesis of various diseases, including cancer [12], neurodegenerative disorders [13], ischemia-reperfusion injury [14], renal diseases [15], and blood disorders [12,16,17]. Therefore, research into the mechanisms and drug development targeting ferroptosis have become central focal points in cancer therapy. Despite recent substantial progress, the functional dynamics and molecular regulatory mechanisms of ferroptosis remain incompletely understood. In this review, we summarize recent advances in ferroptosis research, with a focus on its therapeutic potential in oncology. We discuss current strategies for modulating ferroptosis sensitivity and highlight ferroptosis-targeting compounds under investigation, aiming to guide future translational and clinical efforts [18].

Although the term “ferroptosis” was formally introduced by Dixon et al. in 2012, the underlying concept bears notable resemblance to “oxytosis,” a cysteine depletion-induced form of neuronal cell death first described by Murphy et al. in 1989. This similarity highlights an earlier recognition of the biochemical framework foundational to ferroptotic mechanisms [19]. In oxytosis, neuronal death is triggered by the excitotoxin glutamate, which inhibits the activity of SLC7A11, a key subunit of the cystine–glutamate antiporter System Xc⁻, thereby depleting intracellular cystine and disrupting redox homeostasis, a hallmark event also observed in ferroptosis. Accumulating evidence indicates that oxytosis and ferroptosis share several molecular and biochemical characteristics, such as overlapping gene expression profiles and significant accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which suggest these processes may represent different manifestations of a common regulated cell death pathway [20]. By 2003, a distinct form of non-apoptotic cell death induced by erastin in RAS-expressing cancer cells had garnered increasing attention. Initial characterization revealed that this process was resistant to caspase inhibition and, crucially, could be suppressed by iron chelators, an observation that suggested a dependence on iron and laid the groundwork for the subsequent formal definition of this pathway as the iron-dependent cell death, ferroptosis, nearly a decade later [21]. Subsequent work by Yang et al. showed that RSL3 (RAS-selective lethal small molecule 3) also triggered this type of cell death, further supporting the role of iron as a central mediator. These observations led Dixon et al. to define this non-apoptotic, iron-dependent regulated cell death as “ferroptosis” [22] (Fig. 1). Since then, considerable progress has been made in elucidating the regulatory mechanisms of ferroptosis. Yang et al. identified the glutathione (GSH)–glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) axis as a critical protective pathway against ferroptosis. GPX4 is ubiquitously present in cells and reduces cellular death by countering complex lipid peroxidation. Lipid peroxidation is the process where a ROS damages lipids, and this damage is the key driver of ferroptosis. This process involves the accumulation of lipid peroxides, which destabilizes cell membranes and leads to cell death, and it's a central mechanism in ferroptosis [16,17,23]. Further studies revealed that ACSL4 (Acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4) promotes ferroptosis by facilitating lipid peroxidation [24]. Selenium was also shown to confer protection against ferroptosis by enhancing GPX4 activity [25]. In 2019, two independent studies identified a GPX4-independent antioxidant system involving ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1), coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10), and NAD(P)H, which function cooperatively to inhibit lipid peroxidation [26,27]. Other GPX4-independent protective mechanisms have also been described, including the GCH1 (GTP cyclohydrolase 1)–tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) axis. More recently, Mao et al. reported that the mitochondrial dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH)–CoQ10 pathway suppresses ferroptosis from within the inner mitochondrial membrane [28]. Building upon this, Mishima et al. discovered that vitamin K acts as a potent FSP1-dependent ferroptosis inhibitor, identified through a functional screen of vitamin compounds in GPX4-deficient mouse embryonic fibroblasts [29].

Ferroptosis is a distinct form of regulated cell death orchestrated by a complex interplay among oxidative stress, lipid metabolism, and iron homeostasis. Its biochemical hallmark is the iron-dependent accumulation of lipid peroxides, primarily originating from the peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) within membrane phospholipids [22]. PUFAs, characterized by bis-allylic hydrogen atoms, have bis-allylic C-H bonds that are destabilized by adjacent double bonds, making these sites especially vulnerable to hydrogen abstraction. Once a hydrogen atom is removed, the carbon-centered radicals react rapidly with molecular oxygen, and can also react with iron-derived ROS, especially hydroxyl radicals generated via the Fenton reaction, amplifying oxidative damage. This cascade leads to widespread lipid peroxidation and membrane damage, culminating in cell death [24]. To mitigate iron-mediated oxidative stress, cells tightly regulate iron storage, uptake, and export through proteins such as ferritin, transferrin, ferroportin, transferrin receptor 1 (TFR1), and hepcidin. Another critical defense mechanism is the cystine/glutamate antiporter System Xc⁻, which imports cystine to support the synthesis of GSH, a major intracellular antioxidant. GSH serves as a cofactor for GPX4, an essential enzyme that reduces lipid hydroperoxides to non-toxic lipid alcohols. A defining feature of ferroptosis is the depletion of GSH and inactivation of GPX4, which leads to uncontrolled lipid peroxidation and overwhelming ROS accumulation [4]. While PUFA oxidation is an unavoidable physiological process, ferroptosis arises when the antioxidant defense machinery-particularly the GSH-GPX4 axis-is compromised. This feature sets ferroptosis apart from other forms of PCD, such as apoptosis. Ferroptosis is characterized by a failure to suppress lethal oxidative damage, whereas apoptosis typically proceeds through an actively executed signaling cascade [23,24]. Importantly, recent studies have demonstrated that endocytosis plays a crucial role in cysteine-deprivation-induced ferroptosis. Specifically, the depletion of cysteine leads to the activation of endocytic pathways, which facilitate the uptake of iron into lysosomes. This increase in lysosomal iron levels is a key factor in driving the ferroptotic process. The accumulation of iron within lysosomes enhances the production of ROS through Fenton chemistry, leading to lipid peroxidation and subsequent cell death. These findings underscore the importance of lysosomal iron in the pathogenesis of ferroptosis and highlight the complex interplay between iron metabolism and oxidative stress in this form of regulated cell death [30].

As a regulated form of cell death, ferroptosis is primarily triggered by disruption of the cellular microenvironment. Its most distinctive hallmarks are iron accumulation and ROS production. Its execution depends on the accumulation of lipid peroxides and their uncontrolled propagation, ultimately leading to rupture of the cell membrane [31]. Conceptually, ferroptosis resembles a cellular “fire”: ROS act as the ignition source, iron serves as the blower amplifying the flames, lipid peroxides are the ignited cellular contents, and differing lipid compositions result in varying cellular tolerance to the fire. Under physiological conditions, cells are equipped with robust antioxidant systems (akin to fire extinguishers) that neutralize lipid oxidation and maintain membrane integrity. However, when iron overload or elevated ROS levels overwhelm these protective systems, oxidative damage escalates uncontrollably, ultimately causing membrane rupture and cell demise [32]. Mechanistically, ferroptosis involves several interconnected steps. Mitochondrial metabolism generates hydroxyl radicals, which iron catalyzes through the Fenton reaction to form additional hydroxyl radicals. These hydroxyl radicals then trigger lipid peroxidation by abstracting hydrogen atoms from PUFAs. This process is self-amplifying: excessive ROS promote further radical generation, exacerbating membrane lipid oxidation. The glutathione-dependent enzyme GPX4 plays a central role in detoxifying lipid hydroperoxides and can be regarded as a molecular "firefighter". Loss of GPX4 activity or depletion of glutathione disables this defense, leaving cells vulnerable to oxidative collapse [23,24,33]. Previously, we used to think that ferroptosis did not depend on classical apoptotic mechanisms, but recent studies have shown that caspase-2, a highly conserved member of the caspase family, plays a significant role in modulating ferroptosis. Specifically, caspase-2 protects cancer cells from ferroptotic cell death by regulating the expression of stress response genes, including SESN2, HMOX1, and SLC7A1, which are essential for cellular defense against oxidative stress [6]. The depletion of caspase-2 downregulates these genes, thereby sensitizing mutant-p53 cancer cells to ferroptosis-inducing compounds. Notably, the canonical catalytic activity of caspase-2 is not required for its protective role, suggesting that it regulates ferroptosis through non-proteolytic interactions with other proteins. This study also identified novel caspase-2 interacting proteins, including heat shock proteins and co-chaperones, which further elucidate the complex mechanisms underlying caspase-2's function in ferroptosis. These findings underscore the multifaceted nature of ferroptosis regulation. Ferroptosis is not initiated solely by iron overload or ROS generation in isolation. Instead, this occurs when these specific protein interactions impair the cell antioxidant system. When the antioxidant system remains functional, cells may resist ferroptotic death or undergo alternative regulated cell death pathways [7]. This highlights the critical role of lipid peroxide detoxification in the regulation of ferroptosis and underscores the complexity of the interplay between different cell death pathways.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Importance of ferroptosis in cancer therapy
ce:section.ce:para: Apoptosis has long been regarded as the primary mode of PCD in cancer. However, therapies designed to activate apoptotic pathways have demonstrated limited efficacy in clinical settings, underscoring the urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies that engage alternative cell death mechanisms. In this context, ferroptosis has emerged as a promising target for cancer intervention and has become a focal point of mechanistic and translational research [34]. Ferroptosis is intimately linked to tumor biology. Notably, several tumor suppressor genes exert their anticancer effects, at least in part, by promoting ferroptosis. Multiple tumor suppressors-including p53 and BAP1-have been shown to enhance cellular sensitivity to ferroptosis, suggesting that ferroptosis may serve as an intrinsic tumor-suppressive mechanism. This raises the compelling hypothesis that ferroptosis underpins the tumor-suppressive activity of these genes and that restoring or enhancing ferroptosis sensitivity may provide a therapeutic avenue for malignancies refractory to apoptosis-targeted therapies [35,36]. Conversely, to ensure survival, cancer cells have evolved a series of adaptive programs that suppress ferroptosis. These evasion strategies not only promote tumor progression and treatment resistance but also reveal therapeutic opportunities for cancer intervention by harnessing ferroptosis. Intriguingly, mesenchymal and dedifferentiated cancer cells-typically characterized by resistance to apoptosis and conventional therapies-exhibit heightened sensitivity to ferroptosis. This paradox highlights ferroptosis as a potential Achilles heel in otherwise therapy-refractory cancer cell populations [37]. Consequently, ferroptosis has emerged as a promising target for cancer therapy, particularly in treating refractory tumors. Numerous ferroptosis-based interventions have demonstrated encouraging efficacy, even overcoming resistance to conventional treatments. Moreover, ferroptosis contributes to the tumor-suppressive effects of both radiotherapy and immunotherapy [38–42]. Ferroptosis-based combination therapy represents a highly promising strategy to enhance the efficacy of conventional treatments, overcome therapeutic resistance, and reduce tumor recurrence. However, the role of ferroptosis in tumor suppression is context-dependent, exhibiting seemingly paradoxical effects at different stages of tumor development. For example, during chronic liver injury, persistent ferroptosis of hepatocytes can trigger compensatory proliferation and fibrosis, thereby promoting the initiation of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In this context, ferroptosis acts as a double-edged sword, where its initial pro-tumorigenic effects must be carefully managed to prevent tumor initiation. In contrast, pharmacological induction of ferroptosis in established HCC significantly inhibits tumor growth, underscoring the stage-specific and dualistic nature of ferroptosis in liver carcinogenesis, ferroptosis may promote cancer progression in early-stage patients, but for those with advanced tumors, inducing ferroptosis can enhance the efficacy of chemotherapy [43,44]. This suggests that the timing and context of ferroptosis induction are crucial factors in determining its therapeutic efficacy. Moreover, a study found that ferroptosis inhibitors can suppress tumor growth when administered early, not by directly targeting tumor cells, but by preventing the ferroptosis of tumor-associated neutrophils and thereby relieving immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment [45]. These findings highlight the complexity of ferroptosis in cancer and underscore the importance of context-specific strategies for its therapeutic targeting. It also raises several key unanswered questions that are crucial for advancing the field. For instance, identifying biomarkers for contextual ferroptosis is essential. What biomarkers can be used to predict the stage of tumor development and the likelihood of ferroptosis contributing to tumor initiation versus tumor suppression? Identifying such biomarkers could enable the development of personalized therapeutic strategies that maximize the benefits of ferroptosis while minimizing potential risks. Additionally, optimizing the timing and sequencing of ferroptosis-based therapies is critical. How can we optimize the timing and sequencing of ferroptosis-based therapies to avoid promoting tumor initiation while effectively targeting established tumors? This requires a deeper understanding of the temporal dynamics of ferroptosis in different cancer contexts. Furthermore, designing combination therapies that leverage the anti-tumorigenic effects of ferroptosis while mitigating its pro-tumorigenic potential is another important challenge.

The application of ferroptosis-inducing agents, such as erastin and RSL3, represents a promising therapeutic strategy in oncology. Notably, ferroptosis was first discovered through a synthetic lethal screen in RAS-mutant cancer cells, highlighting its potential relevance in tumors driven by oncogenic RAS. Functional evidence has since demonstrated ferroptosis sensitivity in cancer types characterized by elevated lipid peroxidation, including hepatocellular carcinoma, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), and renal cell carcinoma, indicating that these tumor types may be particularly amenable to ferroptosis-targeted therapies [46–50]. Importantly, ferroptosis has also been implicated in overcoming therapeutic resistance. Several studies have shown that cancer cells in a high-mesenchymal state, while often refractory to conventional treatments, exhibit marked sensitivity to ferroptosis inducers. Furthermore, preconditioning tumors with ferroptosis-inducing compounds has been shown to sensitize cancer cells to subsequent immunotherapies, offering a synergistic avenue for combination treatment strategies [49]. Given the dualistic nature of ferroptosis, how can we design combination therapies that achieve this balance? This involves exploring synergistic interactions between ferroptosis inducers and other therapeutic agents, such as immunotherapies or radiotherapies. Addressing these questions is essential for translating the promise of ferroptosis-based therapies into clinical practice. Future research should focus on elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying the context-dependent effects of ferroptosis and developing strategies to harness its therapeutic potential in a stage-specific manner.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Mechanisms of resistance to ferroptosis in tumor cells

ce:section.ce:para: Erastin and RSL3 represent two prototypical classes of ferroptosis inducers: Erastin acts by inhibiting the cystine/glutamate antiporter System Xc⁻, while RSL3 directly inactivates GPX4 [51]. System Xc⁻, composed of the subunits SLC7A11 and solute carrier family 3 member 2 (SLC3A2), facilitates the import of extracellular cystine in exchange for intracellular glutamate [52,53]. Once transported into the cell, cystine is rapidly reduced to cysteine, a crucial intracellular antioxidant and the rate-limiting substrate for GSH synthesis, catalyzed by glutamate–cysteine ligase (GCL) (Fig. 2A)[54,55]. Cellular availability of GSH tightly regulates GPX4 activity. Consequently, the loss of GPX4 function, whether resulting from indirect GSH depletion through System Xc⁻ inhibition (e.g., by Erastin) or from direct GPX4 inhibition (e.g., by RSL3), underscores its essential role in suppressing ferroptosis [56,57].

GPX4, a selenoprotein, inhibits ferroptosis by reducing lipid hydroperoxides through its catalytic selenocysteine residue. As the catalytic activity of GPX4 is entirely dependent on the incorporation of Sec, this amino acid is considered the 21st amino acid within the context of GPX4 function. It is synthesized via the transfer of activated selenium to a specialized tRNA[Ser]Sec. Given that free selenium is both highly reactive and limited in availability, its intracellular transport is thought to depend on a dedicated carrier system to ensure safe and efficient delivery [16,17,58]. Sec insertion into GPX4 is governed by the Selenocysteine Insertion Sequence (SECIS), an evolutionarily conserved stem-loop in the 3′ untranslated region (3′UTR) that re-programs the UGA stop codon to specify Sec incorporation [59]. Among the glutathione peroxidases, only GPX4 exhibits phospholipid hydroperoxidase activity, converting membrane-bound lipid hydroperoxides (PLOOH) to non-reactive alcohols (PLOH) [60,61]. The enzyme cycles through a redox shuttle cycle: (i) PLOOH oxidizes the active-site selenol (GPX4-SeH) to selenenic acid (GPX4-SeOH). (ii) GSH then attacks GPX4-SeOH to form a selenyl-sulfide adduct (GPX4-Se-SG). (iii) a second GSH regenerates GPX4-SeH concomitant with GSSG production [62]. Crystallographic snapshots have also captured a seleninic acid intermediate (GPX4–Se–OO⁻), suggesting that GPX4 undergoes a three-state redox cycle (GPX4–SeH, GPX4–SeOH, GPX4–Se–OO⁻), rather than the classical two-state mechanism [63]. Consistently, replacing the catalytic Sec with cysteine (U46C) abolishes peroxidase activity and sensitizes cells to ferroptosis, underscoring the indispensable function of selenocysteine in GPX4-mediated cytoprotection [64]. GPX4 possesses three isoforms, localized to mitochondria, cytoplasm, and the nucleus, are generated from a single gene through alternative transcription start sites and are positioned at distinct locations to perform their specific functions [65–68]. Germ-line loss or catalytic inactivation of the cytosolic isoform causes mid-gestation lethality [69], and survival of GPX4-null embryos is restored only when cytoplasmic GPX4 is re-introduced, highlighting its non-redundant role in early development [70,71]. Conversely, deletion of the mitochondrial isoform does not affect overall viability but leads to male sterility due to impaired spermatogenesis [72]. Although cytoplasmic GPX4 was initially considered the primary gatekeeper of ferroptosis, recent studies indicate that mitochondrial GPX4 may play a dominant role in suppressing lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis, particularly in cells deficient in DHODH or glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase 2 (GPD2) [73,74]. These findings suggest that each GPX4 isoform may neutralize hydroperoxides within its specific cellular compartment, while the functional role of nuclear GPX4 remains unclear. Furthermore, loss of GPX4 not only induces ferroptosis but also activates apoptosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis, highlighting lipid peroxidation as a critical nexus among multiple regulated cell death pathways [37]. Therefore, the simultaneous evaluation of multiple ferroptosis biomarkers is essential for the accurate and definitive diagnosis of ferroptosis.

As mentioned above, GPX4 serves as a central suppressor of ferroptosis, and multiple regulatory mechanisms affecting its expression or enzymatic activity critically determine cellular sensitivity to ferroptotic cell death [51,75,76]. Suppression of GPX4 is not always lethal, which led to the identification of three GPX4-bypass pathways that scavenge lipid radicals: the FSP1/CoQH2 axis, the DHODH/CoQH2 module, and the GCH1/BH4 pathway (Fig. 2B). Coenzyme Q exists in oxidized (CoQ10), semiquinone, and fully reduced (CoQH2) forms. The reduced CoQH2 effectively intercepts lipid peroxyl radicals, thereby protecting cells from ferroptosis [39,77]. CoQ10 is synthesized in mitochondria and transported to the plasma membrane by STARD7 (StAR-related lipid transfer domain-containing protein 7) [78]. In 2020, two independent studies demonstrated that N-myristoylation anchors FSP1 to the plasma membrane, where it reduces CoQ10 to CoQH2 using NAD(P)H as an electron donor, thereby preventing lipid peroxidation [77,79,80]. In addition to its role in CoQ10 metabolism, FSP1 also functions as a vitamin K reductase, generating hydroquinones that suppress lipid peroxidation through further consumption of NAD(P)H [81]. Recently, phase-separated FSP1 condensates, dependent on N-terminal myristoylation, specific amino acid residues, and intrinsically disordered regions, have been reported to modulate ferroptosis [82]. Operating in parallel at the cell periphery, mitochondrial DHODH safeguards mitochondrial integrity by reducing CoQ10 to CoQH2 and detoxifying lipid peroxides in situ [73]. GCH1 employs a dual strategy: it produces the lipophilic antioxidant BH4 to inhibit lipid peroxidation and remodels the phospholipidome to maintain polyunsaturated phospholipids containing two acyl tails [79,83]. However, the precise intracellular locales where the GCH1/BH4 system operates remain to be mapped.

The identification of these multiple resistance pathways highlights the complexity of ferroptosis resistance in tumors. Tumors may differentially leverage these pathways depending on their genetic and metabolic contexts. For instance, tumors with high levels of lipid peroxidation may rely more on GPX4 for survival, making them more susceptible to GPX4 inhibitors. In contrast, tumors with lower GPX4 expression or activity may compensate through the FSP1/CoQH2 axis or other GPX4-bypass pathways. Understanding these differential dependencies is crucial for designing effective combination therapies. For example, combining GPX4 inhibitors with agents that target the FSP1/CoQH2 axis could provide a synergistic effect by simultaneously blocking multiple resistance pathways. Similarly, targeting both GPX4 and DHODH could enhance ferroptosis induction in tumors that utilize these pathways. Additionally, the GCH1/BH4 pathway could be targeted in combination with other ferroptosis inducers to further enhance therapeutic efficacy. Future research should focus on elucidating the specific contexts in which each resistance pathway is activated and developing strategies to simultaneously target multiple pathways to overcome resistance and enhance therapeutic outcomes.

Unlike PUFAs, monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) lack bis-allylic carbons, making them inherently resistant to peroxidation. Supplementation with MUFAs can competitively displace PUFAs from membrane phospholipids, thereby reducing the risk of ferroptosis [84]. The key enzymes driving this protective remodeling are stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1 (SCD1) and long-chain fatty acyl-CoA synthetase 3 (ACSL3). SCD1 desaturates newly synthesized palmitate (C16:0) and stearate (C18:0) at the cis-Δ9 position, generating palmitoleate (C16:1) and oleate (C18:1), respectively (Fig. 3A)[85,86]. Elevated SCD1 and ACSL3 activity expands the cellular MUFA pool and confers ferroptosis resistance, whereas SCD1 and ACSL3 blockade sensitizes cells [86,87]. MUFAs additionally promote lipid-droplet formation and peroxisome biogenesis, both of which may sequester or catabolize oxidation-prone ether lipids [88]. Adding oleic acid (a type of MUFA) to the medium can inhibit ferroptosis. Nevertheless, oleic acid loses its protective effect when ACSL3 is deleted [89], underscoring the requirement for ACSL3-mediated conversion of MUFAs into acyl-CoAs prior to membrane insertion (Fig. 3A)[85]. Recently, MBOAT1 and MBOAT2 were shown to selectively incorporate MUFAs into lysophosphatidylethanolamine, increasing PE-MUFA levels at the expense of PE-PUFA. This lipid metabolic process independently regulates ferroptosis via GPX4 or FSP1 [87].

Plasma membrane resealing functions as a late-stage defense against ferroptotic execution [90]. The terminal phase of ferroptosis is characterized by plasma membrane rupture and collapse of the outer mitochondrial membrane [91–93]. Repair mechanisms play a critical role in limiting cell death. Among them, the evolutionarily conserved Endosomal Sorting Complex Required for Transport-III (ESCRT-III) is particularly notable for its ability to protect against multiple forms of regulated cell death, including ferroptosis [94–96]. Lipid peroxidation creates pores in cell membranes, leading to leakage of extracellular Ca²⁺ into the cytoplasm and increasing intracellular Ca²⁺ levels [97], which in turn recruits ESCRT-III components, such as charged multivesicular body proteins CHMP5 and CHMP6, to the plasma membrane for localized repair. Genetic silencing of CHMP5, CHMP6, or CHMP4B has been shown to increase sensitivity to ferroptosis [97,98]. Beyond ferroptosis, ESCRT-III also restricts pore-induced membrane damage during necroptosis and pyroptosis, establishing it as a broad suppressor of non-apoptotic cell death [99,100]. In pancreatic carcinoma models, classical ferroptosis inducers such as erastin and RSL3 promote the accumulation of CHMP5 and CHMP6 at the cell surface, whereas knockout of either protein significantly heightens ferroptotic vulnerability [96]. FSP1 further enhances resistance by facilitating CHMP5 and CHMP6 recruitment to the plasma membrane (Fig. 3B)[101]. However, when lipid peroxidation surpasses a critical threshold, the repair capacity of CHMP4B-, CHMP5-, and CHMP6-mediated pathways is ultimately overwhelmed, leading to cell death [97,98].

Iron is an essential trace element in the body, and its abnormal distribution or content can disrupt normal physiological processes. In circulation, iron exists as Fe³ ⁺ bound to transferrin (TF). The TF–Fe³ ⁺ complex binds to TFR1 and undergoes endocytosis [102]. Inside the cell, Fe³ ⁺ is reduced to Fe²⁺ by six-transmembrane epithelial antigen of the prostate 3 (STEAP3), after which Fe²⁺ is either released into the labile iron pool (LIP) or stored in ferritin. This process is mediated by divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) or zinc-iron regulatory proteins ZIP8 and ZIP14. Excess Fe²⁺ is exported and oxidized back to Fe³ ⁺ by ferroportin (Fig. 3C)[103]. This tightly controlled iron cycle influences cellular sensitivity to ferroptosis: knockdown of TFRC reduces erastin-induced ferroptotic cell death, whereas overexpression of heme oxygenase-1 (HMOX-1) enhances it by increasing intracellular iron availability. Heat shock protein beta-1 (HSPB1) suppresses ferroptosis by downregulating TFR1 and lowering intracellular iron levels (Fig. 3C) [104]. Ferritin, composed of ferritin light chain (FTL) and ferritin heavy chain 1 (FTH1), is transcriptionally upregulated when iron response element binding protein 2 (IREB2) is inhibited. This elevation in ferritin sequesters iron and thereby inhibits erastin-induced ferroptosis [105].

NRF2 serves as a master regulator of cellular antioxidant responses, whose stability is precisely controlled by several E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes, including KEAP1–CUL3–RBX1 (Fig. 4A), SCF/β-TrCP (Fig. 4B), and synoviolin/Hrd1 (Fig. 4C) that target it for proteasomal degradation under homeostatic conditions [106]. Upon activation via genetic alteration, post-translational modification, or pharmacological inhibition, NRF2 accumulates and translocates into the nucleus, where it drives the expression of a battery of genes bearing antioxidant response elements (AREs) (Fig. 4D). These target genes collectively suppress ferroptosis through three core mechanisms: regulating iron homeostasis, reprogramming cellular metabolism, and enhancing glutathione biosynthesis and utilization [107]. A broad spectrum of NRF2 target genes contributes to the suppression of ferroptosis by attenuating lipid peroxidation, which can be functionally grouped into three major categories: (i) Iron and Heme Homeostasis: NRF2 enhances cellular iron storage through upregulation of ferritin heavy and light chains (FTH1/FTL), and promotes iron export via ferroportin (SLC40A1). It also regulates heme metabolism genes including HMOX1, FECH, ABCB6, and SLC48A1, and elevates biliverdin reductases BLVRA/B, collectively reducing iron-catalyzed ROS generation and lipid peroxidation [108]. (ii) Intermediary Metabolism and Redox Balance: NRF2 activation strengthens redox capacity by inducing nuclear receptors (e.g., NROB2, PPARG) and key metabolic enzymes such as aldo-keto reductases (AKR1C1–3, AKR1B1, AKR1B10), ALDH1A1, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), which facilitates NADPH regeneration and promotes reduction–oxidation homeostasis [109]. (iii) Glutathione Synthesis and Utilization: NRF2 comprehensively regulates glutathione metabolism by transcriptionally activating glutamate–cysteine ligase subunits (GCLC/GCLM), glutathione synthetase (GSS), and the cystine/glutamate antiporter SLC7A11, thereby promoting GSH biosynthesis. Furthermore, it upregulates several GSH-dependent enzymes including glutathione S-transferases (GSTs) [110], peroxiredoxins (PRDX1, PRDX6), thioredoxin reductase (TXNRD1), and critically, GPX4, the central guardian against phospholipid peroxidation and ferroptosis [111]. Through the coordinated regulation of iron metabolism, metabolic reprogramming, and glutathione-dependent antioxidant pathways, NRF2 establishes a multi-layered defense system against lipid peroxidation and ferroptotic cell death. Consequently, its dysregulation is implicated in various diseases characterized by oxidative damage and ferroptosis [112].

ce:section.ce:section-title: The induction and execution of ferroptosis

ce:section.ce:para: As a novel iron-driven, regulated, non-apoptotic cell death pathway [113], ferroptosis is characterized by the distinctive biochemical feature of polyunsaturated membrane lipid peroxidation, which distinguishes it from other forms of cell death [114]. The accumulation of these lipid peroxides at toxic levels compromises membrane integrity and ultimately leads to cell death. Any cell containing iron, molecular oxygen, and PUFA-containing phospholipids is inherently susceptible to ferroptosis. To counteract this vulnerability, cells have evolved enzymatic defense systems that prevent the buildup of lipid hydroperoxides [90]. Many classical ferroptosis inducers, including erastin and RSL3, function by disrupting these antioxidant defense mechanisms, highlighting the central role of redox-regulating proteins in ferroptosis suppression [115,116].

Among them, GPX4 is a key enzyme that reduces toxic lipid hydroperoxides (Lipid-ROS) to their corresponding alcohols, thus preventing membrane damage [117,118]. Specifically, GPX4 reduces phospholipid hydroperoxides (e.g., AA/AdA–PE–OOH) to phospholipid alcohols (PLOH), functioning as a phospholipid hydroperoxidase. Its activity is dependent on GSH and selenium availability [115]. Small molecules such as RSL3, ML162, and ML210 directly inhibit GPX4. In contrast, compounds like erastin and FIN56 impair GPX4 activity indirectly by depleting intracellular GSH. RSL3 binds covalently to GPX4, while erastin targets the cystine/glutamate antiporter (System Xc⁻), reducing cysteine uptake and depleting GSH pools [114].

Functioning in parallel to GPX4, ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1/AIFM2) suppresses lipid peroxidation at the plasma membrane. As an NAD(P)H- and FAD-dependent oxidoreductase, FSP1 regenerates reduced CoQH2 and vitamin K hydroquinone (VKH2), both acting as lipophilic radical-trapping antioxidants (RTAs) [90,119,120]. N-myristoylation is essential for FSP1’s translocation to the plasma membrane, where it facilitates CoQH2 regeneration in a GPX4-independent manner [115]. FSP1 activity is specifically inhibited by the small-molecule compound iFSP1 [121]. The System Xc⁻ antiporter, composed of SLC7A11 (light chain) and SLC3A2 (heavy chain), maintains intracellular GSH levels by importing cystine in exchange for glutamate [115]. GSH synthesis is driven by cysteine availability, the activity of GCL, and sulfur amino acid metabolism. Pharmacological inhibition of GCL by buthionine sulfoximine (BSO) induces ferroptosis directly or enhances sensitivity to other ferroptosis triggers [113,122]. Similarly, suppression of SLC7A11 by erastin, sorafenib, sulfasalazine, or excess extracellular glutamate depletes GSH and promotes ferroptotic death [123].

Iron is a pivotal catalyst of lipid peroxidation via the Fenton reaction, making it essential to ferroptosis execution. While mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum have long been recognized as key regulators of ferroptosis due to their metabolic roles, lysosomes have recently emerged as central hubs in ferroptotic signaling. Lysosomal iron, in particular, has been identified as a critical initiator of ferroptosis [124]. Classical ferroptosis inhibitors such as liproxstatin-1 (Lip-1) exert protective effects by inactivating lysosomal iron, thereby reducing oxidative membrane damage. In contrast, inducers like RSL3 preferentially initiate lipid peroxidation at lysosomal membranes, highlighting the organelle’s initiating role in ferroptotic cascades [125]. Building on these insights, researchers have developed lysosome-targeted ferroptosis inducers such as Fentomycin-1 (Fento-1), which activates lysosomal iron to initiate local oxidative phospholipid degradation through enhanced Fenton chemistry. Fento-1 effectively triggers ferroptosis by promoting lysosomal lipid peroxidation, which in turn causes iron leakage into the cytosol. This process increases lysosomal membrane permeability (LMP) and amplifies global lipid peroxidation throughout the cell. Thus, the lysosome is increasingly recognized not as a passive iron reservoir, but as a dynamic and therapeutically targetable node in ferroptosis regulation. Modulating lysosomal iron metabolism offers a promising avenue for future ferroptosis-based therapeutic strategies [126].

Ferroptosis culminates in plasma membrane rupture driven by lipid peroxide accumulation, a terminal event that distinguishes it from apoptosis and aligns it with other non-apoptotic cell death modalities such as necroptosis and pyroptosis. The execution of ferroptosis is tightly regulated by two major antioxidant defense axes: the glutathione–glutathione peroxidase 4 (GSH–GPX4) axis and the NADPH–FSP1 axis, both of which function to suppress membrane lipid peroxidation [90]. In contrast to necroptosis and pyroptosis, which involve membrane pores formed by mixed lineage kinase domain-like pseudokinase (MLKL) and Gasdermin D (GSDMD), respectively, ferroptosis lacks a dedicated pore-forming executor protein [127,128]. Instead, it relies on lipid-driven processes that compromise plasma membrane integrity.

Recent studies implicate Ninjurin-1 (NINJ1) as a critical mediator of plasma membrane rupture (PMR) in ferroptosis. Although NINJ1 is not involved in upstream ferroptotic events such as lipid peroxidation or calcium influx, it promotes membrane disruption through oligomerization, contributing to the final steps of cell lysis[129]. Knockout of NINJ1 confers resistance to ferroptosis-associated PMR, suggesting it acts downstream of lipid peroxidation to facilitate cell membrane swelling and membrane breakdown. Moreover, NINJ1 has been shown to increase the mechanical fragility of the membrane, potentially enhancing susceptibility to rupture in multiple forms of PCD beyond ferroptosis [130]. Its role in mediating the release of cytosolic proteins and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) highlights its potential as an immunomodulatory factor. Notably, the contribution of NINJ1 to ferroptosis appears to be context- and cell type-dependent [131].

Additionally, the mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo1 has been identified as a potential mediator of ferroptosis in specific cellular contexts [132]. Under ferroptosis conditions, lipid peroxidation appears to begin within organelles such as the mitochondria and lysosomes, eventually extending to the plasma membrane [133,134]. Elevated membrane tension from lipid peroxidation activates Piezo1 and TRP channels, inducing characteristic ion fluxes (Ca2+/Na+ influx, K+efflux). These shifts compromise ionic homeostasis, driving osmotic swelling, a critical precursor to membrane rupture. Further exacerbating this dysregulation, Na+/K+-ATPase inactivation likely occurs through altered binding to peroxidized phospholipids [132]. Although plasma membrane rupture can be transiently delayed by polyethylene glycol (PEG), which blocks membrane nanopores and restricts ion and water flow, PEG does not prevent cell death entirely [97,135]. Ultimately, as lipid peroxidation intensifies, the plasma membrane’s biophysical properties become so compromised that rupture is unavoidable [136]. These findings position ferroptosis membrane breakdown as a lipid-centric process involving both biophysical membrane destabilization and regulatory proteins such as NINJ1 and Piezo1.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Mechanisms of tumor cell vulnerability to ferroptosis and strategies to enhance ferroptosis sensitivity
ce:section.ce:para: It is essential to distinguish between ferroptosis sensitivity and the regulation of ferroptosis execution. Ferroptosis sensitivity refers to the inherent susceptibility of a cell to accumulate lethal levels of lipid peroxides within membrane phospholipids. This susceptibility is governed by factors such as intracellular iron availability, ROS and the pool of oxidizable PUFAs, and the capacity of both pro-oxidant and antioxidant systems. A useful conceptual metaphor is to view sensitivity as the combination of “fuel” (PUFAs) and “ignition sources” (iron), while the execution of ferroptosis represents the failure of “fire extinguishers” (antioxidant defenses) to suppress lipid peroxidation, ultimately leading to membrane rupture. Modulating ferroptosis sensitivity involves a wide array of enzymes, biomolecules, and metabolites that influence lipid peroxidation dynamics [90].These components are distributed throughout the cell, including the plasma membrane, cytosol, and various organelles. The contribution of specific metabolites, enzymes, and organelles to both the execution of ferroptosis and the modulation of sensitivity varies considerably across cell types and depending on the ferroptosis stimulus [137]. Therefore, the context-dependent roles of these factors highlight the complexity in predicting cellular responses to ferroptosis induction [90].

PUFAs exhibit inherent vulnerability to peroxidation due to weakened C–H bonds in their bis-allylic methylene groups [138,139]. Contemporary investigations have concentrated on ω-6 species, γ-linolenic (18:3), linoleic (18:2), dihomo-γ-linolenic (20:3), arachidonic (AA, 20:4) and adrenic (AdA, 22:4) acids, along with ω-3 counterparts such as α-linolenic (18:3), eicosapentaenoic (20:5) and docosahexaenoic (22:6) acids [140,141]. Among these, AA (20:4) and AdA (22:4) represent the dominant lipid peroxidation substrates in ferroptosis. Critically, unesterified PUFAs lack intrinsic cytotoxic. Their incorporation into membrane phospholipids requires sequential enzymatic processing: ACSL4-mediated conversion to CoA derivatives followed by LPCAT3-catalyzed esterification to phosphatidylethanolamines (PEs). Illustratively, ACSL4 activates free AA to AA-CoA, which LPCAT3 subsequently esterifies to form PE-AA, an essential step for ferroptosis execution [142–144]. Malonyl-CoA, generated via ACC-dependent carboxylation of acetyl-CoA, facilitates de novo synthesis of specific PUFAs and is likewise necessary for ferroptosis [145]. Peroxisomal biogenesis of plasmalogens constitutes an additional route for generating peroxidizable PUFAs and thereby promotes ferroptosis [146,147]. Conversely, phospholipase A2 group VI (iPLA2β) removes oxidized PUFA moieties from phospholipids, attenuating p53-mediated ferroptosis [148]. Significantly, deuterium substitution at bis-allylic sites in PUFAs (D-PUFAs) retards radical chain propagation and confers resistance to erastin- or RSL3-induced ferroptosis, highlighting structure-dependent reactivity determinants [138] (Fig. 5A).

Lipid peroxidation is the biochemical hallmark of ferroptosis, driven primarily by the oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing phospholipids (PUFA-PLs) [92]. The bis-allylic carbon atoms in these lipids render them particularly susceptible to oxidation, which can occur via both enzymatic and non-enzymatic (autoxidative) mechanisms involving ferrous iron (Fe2+) [138,149]. Among enzymatic routes, lipoxygenases (ALOXs) and cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase (POR) dominate [150].

ALOX enzymes represent a class of non-heme iron dioxygenases that catalyze direct insertion of molecular oxygen into membrane-embedded PUFAs or PUFA-containing phospholipids. ALOX12 is indispensable for p53-mediated ferroptosis, whereas ALOX15, complexed with phosphatidylethanolamine-binding protein 1 (PEBP1), selectively targets stearoyl-AA-PE to produce lethal lipid peroxides during erastin- or RSL3-induced death [151]. Additional ALOX family members, including ALOXE3, ALOX5, ALOX12B and ALOX15B, also participate in ferroptotic signaling [152–154]. Pharmacological blockade of multiple ALOXs attenuates lipid peroxidation and affords cytoprotection [155,156]. Nevertheless, genetic ablation of ALOX15 in GPX4-knockout mice fails to block ferroptosis in vivo, and combined ALOX12 and ALOX15 deficiency fails to rescue GPX4-null T-cell viability, indicating that compensatory pathways can sustain lipid peroxidation in specific contexts [16,17,93,157]. In parallel, cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase (POR) supports non-ALOX-driven peroxidation by providing reducing equivalents to cytochrome P450 enzymes, illustrating the redundancy in enzymatic peroxidation pathways [150,158]. Regarding non-enzymatic mechanisms, iron-catalyzed Fenton chemistry primarily mediates PUFA-phospholipid peroxidation [149,159]. The reaction cascade initiates when GPX4 fails to reduce nascent phospholipid hydroperoxides (PLOOHs), whether enzymatically generated or arising from metabolic processes. Subsequent interaction of PLOOHs with ferrous iron (Fe2+) produces alkoxyl (RO•) and peroxyl (ROO•) radicals via Fenton reactions, thereby propagating autocatalytic PLOOHs formation [160,161] (Fig. 5B). Collectively, these findings highlight that lipid peroxidation during ferroptosis can be initiated and amplified through multiple enzyme-dependent and iron-catalyzed pathways. Future studies are warranted to identify additional oxygenases and contextual factors that influence peroxidation dynamics in different biological settings.

As highlighted earlier, lipid peroxidation relies on both iron-activated enzymes and iron-driven Fenton chemistry, underscoring the obligatory role of iron in ferroptosis. This notion is further supported by recent findings that endocytosis is essential for cysteine-deprivation-induced ferroptosis, indicating that lysosomal iron may also play a critical role in this process [30]. Consequently, any manipulation of iron trafficking modulates ferroptosis risk. Circulating Fe3+ is bound to transferrin [162] and internalized via the membrane receptor TFR1 [163], within the endosome it is reduced to Fe²⁺ by STEAP3 [164], then released into the cytosol through SLC11A2 to constitute the labile iron pool that fuels hydroxyl radical formation and ensuing ferroptosis [165]. Excess iron is ordinarily locked inside ferritin, a heteropolymer of FTH1 and FTL [166]. However, nuclear receptor coactivator 4 (NCOA4)-mediated ferritin phagocytosis releases a large amount of free iron [91,167], whereas SLC40A1 exports surplus Fe2+ across the membrane [168]. Consistent with this circuitry, genetic ablation of TF, TFR1, SLC11A2 or NCOA4, together with enforced expression of FTH1, FTL and SLC40A1, all diminish the labile iron pool and thereby blunt ferroptosis [35,169,170]. Thus, interventions that fine-tune cytosolic iron import, storage and export critically calibrate cellular ferroptosis susceptibility.

Beyond the cytoplasmic compartment, mitochondria serve as the principal hub for iron utilization and the dominant source of ROS, critically regulating redox-active processes and ferroptosis [162,171]. Iron entry into the mitochondrial matrix requires sequential transport through both outer and inner membranes, mediated by SLC11A2 on the outer membrane and by solute carrier family 25 member 37 (SLC25A37) or solute carrier family 25 member 28 (SLC25A28) on the inner membrane [172–175]. Recent investigations have emphasized the gatekeeper function of CDGSH iron-sulfur domain 1 (CISD1) in mitochondrial iron homeostasis [176,177]. CISD1 depletion markedly augments erastin-induced mitochondrial ferrous iron, amplifying local lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis [178]. Mechanistically, CISD1 interacts with voltage-dependent anion channels (VDACs) and modulates their conductance in a redox-sensitive manner [179]. Pharmacological targeting of VDAC abrogates mitoCISD1-mediated mitochondrial iron loading and erastin-triggered ferroptosis [180,181]. Within the matrix, ferritin mitochondrial (FTMT) sequesters excess iron, thereby lowering both total and chelatable iron and attenuating ferroptosis [59,182,183]. ATP binding cassette subfamily B member 7 (ABCB7) is responsible for exporting iron from mitochondria to the cytosol [184–186]. However, although ABCB7 depletion causes mitochondrial iron accumulation, this condition does not enhance mitochondrial ROS production or induce ferroptosis [184,187]. Conversely, ABCB8 actively exports mitochondrial iron [188,189], and its overexpression reduces matrix iron, conferring protection against ferroptosis-associated ischemia–reperfusion injury and doxorubicin-induced cardiomyopathy [190,191] (Fig. 5C). Recent studies have further elucidated the critical role of 3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase type 2 (BDH2) in mediating iron transfer from lysosomes to mitochondria, which significantly influences ferroptosis susceptibility in melanoma cells [192]. BDH2 localizes at mitochondria-lysosome contact sites (MLCs) and catalyzes the production of 2,5-dihydroxybenzoic acid (2,5-DHBA), a key metabolite that promotes iron translocation from lysosomes to mitochondria. This iron redistribution is essential for sustaining mitochondrial bioenergetics and maintaining lysosomal acidification, thereby supporting MLC stability. The expression and activity of BDH2 vary between melanocytic (MEL) and mesenchymal (MES) states of melanoma cells, contributing to their differential sensitivity to ferroptosis. Specifically, BDH2 deficiency in MES cells disrupts lysosomal pH homeostasis and impairs MLC dynamics, resulting in lysosomal iron accumulation and enhanced ferroptosis vulnerability. Importantly, restoration of BDH2 expression or exogenous administration of 2,5-DHBA normalizes lysosomal acidity and MLC integrity, thereby conferring protection against ferroptosis and promoting metastatic capacity in MES cells. Taken together, these data underscore that multiple, compartment-specific regulators of mitochondrial iron flux collectively dictate cellular susceptibility to ferroptosis.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Tumor suppressors or oncogene control ferroptosis sensitivity
ce:section.ce:para: Mutated in approximately half of all cancers, the tumor suppressor p53 was among the first shown to influence ferroptosis susceptibility. Initial evidence connecting p53 to ferroptosis emerged from studies on a mouse model with triple mutations (K117R, K161R, K162R) in the p53 DNA-binding domain (p53–3KR mice). Remarkably, cells from these mice, deficient in apoptosis and cell cycle arrest, maintain resistance to spontaneous tumor formation via a metabolically adaptive process [193]. Further investigation revealed that this tumor suppression relied on inhibiting the transcription of SLC7A11, the gene for System Xc⁻'s substrate-specific subunit. Silencing SLC7A11 was sufficient to enhance cancer cell vulnerability to oxidative damage, leading to ferroptosis-like death. Furthermore, the discovery of an additional acetylation site (K98) proved critical: when mutated in combination with the other sites, the resulting p53 variant lost its ability to interact with the SLC7A11 promoter. Consequently, these mice exhibited tumor development akin to p53-null animals [194], unlike the tumor-resistant p53–3KR mice. These findings demonstrate that p53-mediated tumor suppression critically relies on ferroptosis induction through SLC7A11 regulation. A subsequent study revealed that the P47S polymorphism prevalent in individuals of African descent increases cancer incidence in mouse models and renders cells ferroptosis-resistant through altered glutamine metabolism [195]. While heightened ferroptosis sensitivity plays a pivotal role in p53-mediated tumor suppression, a key question remains: which physiological trigger initiates the ferroptosis cascade? Current hypotheses suggest that hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), produced by natural killer (NK) cells via NADPH oxidase 2 (NOX2), may serve as a plausible candidate [196]. Additionally, emerging evidence implicates p53 in ferroptosis regulation through its modulation of the mevalonate pathway. During metabolic stress, p53 upregulates ATP-binding cassette subfamily A member 1 (ABCA1), which facilitates cholesterol retrotranslocation from the plasma membrane to the endoplasmic reticulum. This process subsequently inactivates sterol regulatory element-binding protein 2 (SREBP2), thereby suppressing mevalonate pathway activity [197]. SREBP2 inhibition represses mevalonate-gene transcription, lowering squalene and ubiquinone, metabolites previously linked to ferroptosis resistance [198]. Inhibition of the mevalonate pathway may render cells intrinsically susceptible to ferroptosis, provided that key intermediates are not exogenously supplemented. Supporting this notion, studies in a KRAS-G12D and mutant p53-driven murine lung cancer model revealed that the p53-R270H variant exerts a dominant-negative effect over wild-type p53, resulting in elevated expression of SREBP2-regulated genes and heightened sensitivity to statin-induced HMG-CoA reductase inhibition [42]. Intriguingly, this aligns with findings that statins preferentially target ferroptosis-prone cells [21], implying that tumors harboring the p53-R270H mutation, particularly in this context, may be vulnerable to ferroptosis-directed therapies [199].

Emerging evidence reveals an additional layer of complexity: under certain settings, wild-type p53 may confer cytoprotection by paradoxically reinforcing antioxidant capacity. Activation of p21 (Cdkn1a) by p53 has been shown to restrain phospholipid oxidation through preservation of intracellular thiols, including GSH [200]. This observation aligns with an earlier finding that serine deprivation triggers the p53–p21 axis, rerouting serine from nucleotide synthesis toward GSH maintenance [201]. An additional anti-ferroptotic mechanism has been proposed whereby p53 sequesters dipeptidyl peptidase 4 (DPP4), disrupting the NOX1–DPP4 complex at the plasma membrane thereby attenuates ferroptosis. Collectively, these data indicate that p53-mediated ferroptosis modulation is tumor-type- and context-dependent, underscoring the necessity for tissue-specific and condition-specific interpretations [202].

Beyond p53, emerging evidence implicates the tumor suppressor BRCA1-associated protein 1 (BAP1) in ferroptosis regulation [203]. BAP1, frequently inactivated in mesotheliomas (36–65 %), uveal melanomas (32–47 %), cholangiocarcinomas (20–30 %), and clear cell renal cell carcinomas (ccRCCs: 10–15 %), functions as a nuclear deubiquitinase (DUB) that assembles the polycomb repressive deubiquitinase (PR-DUB) complex. This complex catalyzes histone H2A mono-deubiquitylation (H2A-ub), modulating gene expression. Notably, BAP1-mediated H2A-ub targets multiple metabolic genes, with SLC7A11 being significantly downregulated. This suppression of SLC7A11 enhances cellular vulnerability to ferroptosis, synergizing with other tumor-suppressive mechanisms. Recent studies in BAP1-deficient mice further reveal upregulated mevalonate pathway genes and altered lipid metabolism, mirroring metabolic changes observed in p53-deficient models [204] (Fig. 6A).

The convergence of distinct oncogenic pathways on cysteine metabolism and mevalonate signaling underscores a potential common vulnerability to GPX4 inhibition across cancer types. These observations motivate systematic inquiries into whether analogous cystine-uptake deficits and reduced mevalonate intermediates manifest in other cancer contexts, and whether additional tumor suppressors enforce this metabolic state [16,17,205].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Regulation of ferroptosis sensitivity by hypoxia-inducible factors
ce:section.ce:para: Initial analyses of ferroptosis sensitivity in cancer cell lines revealed pronounced GPX4 dependence in renal cell carcinomas (RCCs), yet the molecular drivers of this vulnerability have only recently been clarified [206]. In clear cell RCC (ccRCC), the most frequent RCC subtype, VHL loss renders tumors acutely sensitive to GSH depletion-induced ferroptosis, an effect partly linked to reduced β-oxidation. Intriguingly, both the original authors and an independent group [49] documented marked up-regulation of arachidonate 5-lipoxygenase (ALOX5) in VHL-deficient ccRCC cells, implying heightened inflammatory signalling via ALOX5-derived eicosanoids [207]. Emerging evidence indicates that the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) pathway critically regulates this susceptibility. Specifically, HIF2α promotes ACSL4-mediated polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) accumulation in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). Notably, HIF2α robustly upregulates PTGS2, encoding prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 2, which may facilitate immune evasion through intratumoral prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) production. Intriguingly, the epigenetic regulator HELLS has also been implicated in ferroptosis suppression by stabilizing HIF1α. This occurs via the DNA methylation modifier lymphoid-specific helicase (HELLS)-mediated inhibition of PHD2/EGLN1, leading to transcriptional activation of lipid metabolic genes [207]. Future studies must therefore delineate the distinct and overlapping contributions of HIF transcription factors to ferroptosis control. In parallel, extracellular glutamate exported via System Xc⁻ has been shown to act as a paracrine cue that activates HIF1α in breast cancer, excess glutamate retro-inhibits System Xc⁻, lowering intracellular cysteine and enhancing PHD2 oxidation [208]. Thus, the elevated SLC7A11 expression observed in TNBC may co-operate with heightened HIF1α and HIF2α activity. Activation of these HIF isoforms in TNBC was further shown to require elevated endoplasmic-reticulum-derived X-box binding protein 1 (XBP1) following oestrogen receptor loss [209], aligning with the observation that TNBC cells accumulate PUFAs through ACSL4 [7]. Notably, both ccRCC and TNBC, despite utilizing distinct signaling pathways, ultimately establish a shared metabolic phenotype characterized by ACSL4-mediated PUFA enrichment and prominent lipid droplet accumulation. These lipid droplets serve as dynamic storage depots for arachidonic acid (AA) and other PUFAs, which are utilized not only during nutrient deprivation but also for generating bioactive lipid signaling molecules including eicosanoids [210] (Fig. 6B). Moreover, in astrocytes lipid droplets have been proposed to enhance survival by sequestering lipid hydroperoxides [211].

Emerging studies link non-mutational, mesenchymal-like, therapy-refractory states to increased sensitivity to ferroptosis. An independent report describes how cancer cells adopt a state that is inherently conducive to ferroptosis. Systematic chemical-genetic profiling revealed a high-mesenchymal signature driven by zinc-finger E-box binding homeobox 1 (ZEB1) [212], paralleled by GPX4 dependency in cell lines bearing an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transcriptional program [57]. In addition, clinical concentrations of first-line chemotherapeutics consistently generate persistent residual cell populations across models of melanoma, breast, and lung cancer. These therapy-resistant cells acquire stem-like characteristics and undergo partial mesenchymal transition, as evidenced by their distinctive transcriptional signature [213]. Analogously, melanoma differentiation plasticity dictates BRAF inhibitor responsiveness: differentiated tumors respond to vemurafenib, whereas vemurafenib-induced dedifferentiation heightens ferroptosis susceptibility and immune evasion via loss of melanocyte antigens [214]. Interestingly, vemurafenib-mediated dedifferentiation renders melanoma cells more susceptible to ferroptosis while concurrently promoting immune evasion through downregulation of melanocyte differentiation antigens. Concordantly, vemurafenib-treated melanomas accumulate PUFAs [215]. Within this framework, investigating the regulatory mechanisms governing ferroptosis-associated enzymes (notably ACSL4) may elucidate fundamental processes driving cellular susceptibility to ferroptosis. While the molecular drivers of poorly differentiated states and their ferroptosis vulnerability remain incompletely characterized, emerging evidence implicates ZEB1 as a critical mediator. This transcription factor not only promotes tumor cell stemness, metastatic potential, and metabolic adaptability [216], but also serves as a master regulator of lipid metabolic reprogramming across experimental systems. Although the precise mechanisms remain unclear, this phenotypic effect-overlapping with the dependency on GPX4-may arise from the complex lipidomic remodeling orchestrated by ZEB1 [16,17,217]. Notably, additional regulators of stemness-associated ferroptosis sensitivity likely exist beyond ZEB1. Systematic investigation across experimental models is required to quantify ZEB1's specific contributions and establish definitive mechanistic connections between stem cell programs and enhanced ferroptosis vulnerability [218] (Fig. 6C).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Current and potential therapeutic agents targeting ferroptosis
Overview of promising drugs and targets
ce:section.ce:para: Erastin, belonging to the first generation of ferroptosis inducers, exerts its effect by directly blocking the System Xc⁻ cystine/glutamate antiporter. Although its pro-ferroptotic activity has been extensively validated in vitro across various malignant cancer cell lines, erastin's clinical translation has been impeded by poor in vivo efficacy. To address these limitations, Yang et al. introduced a piperazine moiety into the aniline ring of erastin, generating piperazine erastin, which exhibited improved water solubility and metabolic stability [4]. This derivative effectively suppressed tumor growth in HT-1080 fibrosarcoma xenograft models without notable systemic toxicity. However, its moderate potency limited its efficacy against more advanced tumors. To enhance therapeutic performance, imidazole ketone erastin (IKE) was developed, displaying nanomolar potency and robust metabolic stability [219]. IKE demonstrated significant antitumor activity in SUDHL6 diffuse large B-cell lymphoma xenografts. Furthermore, leveraging its solubility under acidic aqueous conditions, nanoparticle-based delivery systems were employed to increase its therapeutic index and reduce off-target toxicity compared to free IKE [220]. In addition to its standalone effects, erastin has been shown to sensitize multiple cancer cell lines to conventional chemotherapeutic agents, including doxorubicin, actinomycin D, cisplatin, temozolomide, and cytarabine, providing a compelling rationale for combination treatment strategies. However, it should be noted that systemic induction of ferroptosis may carry risks in certain patient populations, such as those with chronic inflammatory conditions, which are often associated with elevated oxidative stress and may predispose to off-target cytotoxicity or unintended tissue damage. Recently, high-resolution structural elucidation of human System Xc⁻ in complex with erastin and IKE confirmed their potent ferroptosis-inducing capabilities and established a molecular basis for the rational design of next-generation ferroptosis-targeting compounds [22,221] (Table 1).

Several small-molecule compounds have been identified as potent ferroptosis inducers, primarily through the inhibition of key regulators such as GPX4 or the depletion of GSH. One of the earliest and most well-characterized agents is RSL3, initially discovered through high-throughput chemical screening. RSL3 induces ferroptosis independently of GSH depletion, instead functioning through direct covalent inhibition of GPX4. This molecular mechanism was confirmed via affinity-based chemoproteomics, which identified GPX4 as its primary binding target. Functional studies further validated this interaction: GPX4 knockdown sensitized cells to RSL3, while GPX4 overexpression conferred resistance [4,16,17,222,223]. RSL3 has since become a widely used tool for inducing ferroptosis in vitro across various cancer types, including pancreatic cancer, adrenocortical carcinoma, fibrosarcoma, and breast cancer. Moreover, RSL3 enhances the efficacy of chemotherapeutic agents such as cisplatin, doxorubicin, and actinomycin D in models of neuroblastoma, osteosarcoma, lung cancer, and rhabdomyosarcoma. In preclinical xenograft models, RSL3 demonstrated favorable safety, showing no significant toxicity or weight loss even at doses as high as 400 mg/kg. Nonetheless, caution is warranted when considering RSL3 or similar agents in the context of predisposed inflammatory microenvironments, where ferroptotic stress could exacerbate tissue injury or promote pro-tumorigenic signaling. Beyond oncology, RSL3 has been instrumental in elucidating ferroptotic mechanisms in disease models such as acute kidney injury (AKI), ischemia/reperfusion injury, and neurodegenerative disorders [31,49,224]. Like RSL3, ML162 was also identified as a covalent GPX4 inhibitor, targeting the enzyme via a reactive alkyl chloride group. However, concerns about selectivity and pharmacokinetic properties spurred the development of ML210, a nitrile oxide-based GPX4 inhibitor with improved pharmacological attributes and comparable potency [210] (Table 1).

Despite these advances, in vivo efficacy of GPX4 inhibitors remains limited, prompting continued efforts to develop compounds with enhanced bioavailability and tumor selectivity [16,17]. Recent studies have highlighted the potential of combining GPX4 inhibitors with BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) to enhance the efficacy of ferroptosis induction in BCR-ABL+ leukemia [16]. Specifically, the use of disulfiram (DSF) in combination with TKIs has shown significant promise. DSF induces ferroptosis by destabilizing GPX4, a key regulator of ferroptosis, thereby increasing intracellular iron levels and lipid peroxidation, which ultimately leads to cell death. This combination therapy has demonstrated the ability to selectively target and eliminate leukemia stem cells (LSCs) and drug-resistant cells, which are often responsible for treatment failure and disease relapse. In preclinical models, this dual targeting strategy significantly improved survival rates, suggesting its potential as a novel therapeutic approach to overcome treatment resistance in BCR-ABL+ leukemia. These findings underscore the importance of GPX4 as a therapeutic target and highlight the potential of combining ferroptosis-inducing agents with existing tyrosine kinase inhibitors to enhance treatment efficacy in leukemia and potentially other cancers.

Fin56, classified as a type III ferroptosis inducer, initiates ferroptotic cell death by promoting the degradation of GPX4 through a mechanism that remains incompletely characterized. In bladder cancer cells, Fin56 has been shown to induce both ferroptosis and autophagy, with emerging evidence indicating that autophagic processes are essential for Fin56-induced ferroptosis. Specifically, pharmacological inhibition of autophagy at various stages attenuated Fin56-triggered oxidative stress and GPX4 degradation, underscoring the dependence of ferroptotic execution on the autophagic machinery. To further explore this interplay, the combinatorial effects of Fin56 and Torin 2, a potent inhibitor of mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) that induces autophagy, were evaluated in bladder cancer models. The results demonstrated a synergistic cytotoxic effect when Fin56 was combined with Torin 2, suggesting that autophagy activation enhances Fin56-mediated ferroptotic cell death. These findings highlight a context-dependent crosstalk between ferroptosis and autophagy, and support the potential of autophagy modulators to augment ferroptosis-based therapeutic strategies in bladder cancer [225]. However, the dual induction of autophagy and ferroptosis may also amplify cellular stress in non-malignant tissues, particularly in conditions characterized by chronic inflammation or degenerative processes. In such conditions, cells are already under significant stress due to ongoing inflammatory responses or the progressive loss of cellular function. The induction of autophagy, while generally a protective mechanism aimed at clearing damaged organelles and misfolded proteins, can become overwhelming if not properly regulated. Similarly, the induction of ferroptosis can further exacerbate cellular stress. When both pathways are activated simultaneously, the combined effects can lead to an overburdening of the cellular stress response mechanisms.
